paragraphs: Spiking Transformers combine attention mechanisms with event-driven neural computation, aiming to retain the energy advantages of spikes while improving predictive performance. Their accuracy still trails conventional neural networks. This paper examines whether part of that gap comes from how the models are optimized, complementing research focused on changing their architecture.

The researchers define noise in parameter updates and use theoretical analysis and experiments to substantiate an excessive-noise problem during training. Their optimizer, AdaS, adaptively adds a gradient update component to adaptive optimization. Its aim is to regulate noise rather than eliminate it: some noise can help a trained model generalize, while too much can interfere with learning.

Experiments across several Spiking Transformer architectures and datasets in vision and natural language processing report consistent performance improvements. These findings support optimizer design as a practical route toward narrowing the accuracy gap with conventional networks while preserving spike-based computation. The contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of training behavior and an optimization method tailored to that diagnosis.
icml-2026-adas-adaptive-gradient-descent.tldr: AdaS improves Spiking Transformer training by adaptively regulating parameter-update noise while retaining its generalization benefits.

paragraphs: AgentWebBench studies a web where a user's agent gets information by communicating with agents operated by individual websites. This changes the task from searching a directly accessible collection into coordinating with intermediaries. The benchmark measures how well the user agent gathers and combines information through these controlled interfaces.

Its four tasks cover search, recommendation, question answering, and deep research. Across seven language models and three coordination strategies, decentralized coordination generally performs worse than centralized retrieval, where the corpus is directly accessible. However, larger models narrow that gap, and the decentralized approach can outperform centralized retrieval on question answering in the reported evaluations.

The experiments also reveal how coordination affects information access. Traffic becomes concentrated on a small number of websites, while additional computation at evaluation time improves interaction reliability and task performance. Successful agents need enough interactions and careful planning. Failure analysis identifies complementary needs: user agents must improve planning and answer synthesis, while website agents must improve retrieval reliability and the quality of evidence they provide.
icml-2026-agentwebbench-benchmarking-mul.tldr: AgentWebBench measures web information gathering through cooperating agents and identifies planning, interaction, and evidence quality as central challenges.

paragraphs: This paper asks when limited labeled data should be used to correct a fixed black-box predictor. Its formal setting assumes that the target function lies within an unknown distance δ of that predictor, measured using the input distribution. The challenge is to exploit a useful starting point without making predictions worse through an unreliable correction.

The analysis characterizes the best achievable worst-case error with finite data. It finds a transition at δ of order n raised to −β/(2β+d), with leading risk given by the smaller of δ squared and n raised to −2β/(2β+d). This distinguishes regimes where proximity to the existing predictor or learning from labeled samples determines the leading error.

The Safe Residual Estimator starts with a zero correction and uses held-out data to decide whether to retain a learned adjustment or revert to the original predictor. It matches the leading theoretical rate plus a validation-selection cost. Synthetic experiments confirm the transition; image and text experiments provide additional practical evidence beyond the formal squared-loss regression setting.
icml-2026-black-box-assisted-regression-.tldr: The paper characterizes when correcting a black-box predictor helps and proposes validation-based residual learning to avoid negative transfer.

paragraphs: Running vision-language-action models on robots requires timely decisions within cost and energy budgets. This paper evaluates models together with the hardware that executes them, including edge accelerators. Its cross-accelerator leaderboard compares cost, energy, and time, showing that suitably sized edge devices can meet control-rate requirements more efficiently than flagship GPUs.

Detailed hardware analysis identifies two distinct phases of inference. The vision-language backbone is limited mainly by computation, whereas the action-producing component is limited mainly by memory access. These different demands cause hardware resources to be underused at different stages. Understanding the phases therefore helps explain why a powerful accelerator does not automatically provide an efficient deployment.

The researchers use those findings to develop DP-Cache and V-AEFusion, targeting repeated diffusion computation and enabling asynchronous pipeline parallelism. They report speedups of up to 2.9 times on GPUs and six times on edge NPUs, with marginal degradation in success. The results connect hardware selection and inference optimization to the practical requirements of on-robot control.
icml-2026-characterizing-vision-language.tldr: Joint model and hardware analysis enables more efficient robot deployment, with targeted optimizations delivering substantial reported inference speedups.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting models can learn misleading fluctuations when their training data contain noise. DropoutTS addresses this by adjusting how strongly the model learns from each sample. The central idea is to vary dropout according to estimated noise, providing a lightweight alternative to removing data or relying on expensive prior noise measurements.

The method uses spectral sparsity to estimate noise through reconstruction residuals: the differences left after reconstructing an instance provide a signal of its noise level. That estimate determines a sample-specific dropout rate, which changes the model's effective learning capacity. The intended balance is to suppress spurious fluctuations while retaining the fine detail needed for accurate forecasting.

Across open benchmarks and different noise regimes, the reported experiments show consistent improvements to strong forecasting backbones. The method adds negligible parameter overhead and requires no architectural changes, making it a plug-in for existing models. Its contribution is a connection between instance-level noise estimation and training regularization, allowing the learning process to respond differently to samples with different noise characteristics.
icml-2026-dropoutts-sample-adaptive-drop.tldr: DropoutTS adjusts dropout for each time-series sample using estimated noise, improving reported forecasting robustness with negligible parameter overhead.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning asks a language model to forget selected information while retaining other capabilities. Those objectives can push parameter updates in conflicting directions. DualOptim+ addresses this tension through the optimizer's internal state, providing a way to share information between objectives while preserving what is specific to each one.

The framework separates optimizer state into a common base and objective-specific delta states. The base captures representations shared by forgetting and retaining, while the deltas preserve their distinct residual components. The optimizer adapts the relationship between shared and separate states according to the directional conflict between the two gradients. This makes the degree of sharing responsive to the objectives' current interaction.

The authors also introduce an 8-bit variant that reduces memory overhead without compromising performance in their reported results. Experiments cover fictitious and real-world unlearning, safety alignment, and multi-task learning, with consistently better trade-offs between objectives. These findings suggest that managing common and objective-specific optimizer information can improve competing-objective training across the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-dualoptim-bridging-shared-and-.tldr: DualOptim+ adapts shared and objective-specific optimizer states to improve the balance between forgetting and retaining information.

paragraphs: Streaming video narration requires a model to describe incoming footage while managing what it remembers from earlier frames. Existing online adaptations can accumulate resource demands as videos get longer. FlowNar addresses this scaling problem by controlling historical visual context while retaining useful information about the stream's past.

Its dynamic context management removes historical visual context, while the Cross Linear Attentive Memory module retains visual history. Together, these components keep visual memory usage and computational complexity bounded. The approach matters because simply retaining more previous footage makes extended streaming increasingly expensive; FlowNar instead explicitly manages the relationship between current context and stored history.

The paper also introduces a self-conditioned evaluation protocol and complementary metrics intended to resemble deployment conditions. Tests on Ego4D, EgoExo4D, and EpicKitchens100 report better narration quality than strong baselines alongside substantial efficiency gains. FlowNar supports videos ten times longer and achieves three times higher throughput in the reported comparisons. These findings show that controlling historical context can improve practical streaming capacity without sacrificing narration quality in those evaluations.
icml-2026-flownar-scalable-streaming-nar.tldr: FlowNar combines visual context removal with retained streaming memory to improve narration quality and scale to longer videos.

paragraphs: A model can score highly on questions about another person's beliefs or intentions without reliably reasoning about their mind. This paper shows that spurious causal correlations can support accuracy as high as 99% on theory-of-mind tasks. It develops a framework for detecting such shortcuts and finds questions reducible to state tracking especially vulnerable.

The researchers then compare supervised fine-tuning with Thinking-RFT, which combines reinforcement learning, verifiable rewards, and explicit reasoning chains. They use four shortcut-free datasets spanning three theory-of-mind contexts. Thinking-RFT improves performance across the evaluated scenarios, with reported gains over supervised fine-tuning of 6% overall, 10% for complex higher-order reasoning, and 7% for multimodal cases.

Thinking-RFT also generalizes better to unseen domains and higher-order questions and shows greater robustness to counterfactuals. Its average 7% advantage over reinforcement fine-tuning without explicit thinking supports the joint contribution of reasoning and reinforcement learning. The analysis links improvement to reasoning grounded in causally relevant cues, including keywords and state changes, making shortcut-resistant evaluation central to interpreting the gains.
icml-2026-from-shortcuts-to-reasoning-ro.tldr: Shortcut-resistant evaluations show that reinforcement fine-tuning with explicit reasoning improves theory-of-mind performance and generalization.

paragraphs: Text-to-SQL systems must identify which database tables and columns are relevant to a user's question. Selecting elements mainly by textual similarity can discard bridge tables whose names seem unimportant but whose relationships are essential for joining data. Graph-Link treats this as a structural problem in addition to a language-matching problem.

The framework represents the schema as a hierarchical graph and selects a constrained subgraph rather than retrieving elements independently. A Steiner-tree-based optimization preserves connections among relevant schema elements while aiming to give the downstream language model a focused selection. Its connectivity guarantee addresses the specific failure where useful tables are retrieved but the relational paths between them are missing.

Experiments on BIRD and Spider 2.0 report state-of-the-art schema linking, with recall and hit-rate improvements of up to 7.0% over competitive baselines. Accuracy on downstream SQL generation for complex queries improves by 13.8%. These results indicate that preserving relational structure during schema selection can help the later generation stage construct successful multi-hop queries.
icml-2026-graph-link-bridging-the-semant.tldr: Graph-Link selects connected schema subgraphs so text-to-SQL systems retain bridge tables needed for complex joins.

paragraphs: Language models can respond differently when prompts are reworded even though their meaning stays the same. This paper investigates whether robustness to such ordinary variations can be improved without expensive retraining of the entire model. It combines theoretical analysis with experiments to identify a targeted intervention.

The analysis highlights perturbation-induced bias: prompt changes can produce a systematic expected shift in the outputs of neural-network modules. That finding motivates a fine-tuning procedure called debiasing for robustness. By targeting the systematic shift associated with meaning-preserving variations, the method connects a measurable internal effect to the desired stability of model behavior.

The paper identifies conditions under which debiasing helps and conditions under which it does not. Its theoretical and experimental findings therefore support a conditional benefit, rather than a universal remedy for prompt sensitivity. Within the studied setting, debiasing may provide a quick and efficient way to improve robustness and certify protection against random prompt perturbations. That certification concerns the random perturbations considered by the analysis, preserving the scope of the paper's claim.
icml-2026-harnessing-non-adversarial-rob.tldr: Targeted debiasing can improve robustness to meaning-preserving prompt changes under identified conditions, with certification against random perturbations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs that differ from its training distribution while preserving performance on familiar data. This paper develops a Probably Approximately Correct learning theory for transformer-based detection. It identifies conditions on data distributions and model configurations under which outliers can be represented and distinguished accurately with sufficient data.

The authors use the relationship between those theoretical requirements and practical training to motivate auxiliary outliers. Their proposed algorithm penalizes outlier misclassification in the training loss and introduces strategically generated soft synthetic outliers. These additions are intended to refine the boundary between familiar inputs and outliers, translating the theory into a training procedure.

The resulting learnability claim is tied to the conditions established by the analysis; it does not assert that every transformer can distinguish arbitrary unfamiliar data. In experiments across different data formats, the algorithm consistently achieves reported state-of-the-art performance. The contribution connects a conditional account of when detection can be learned with an empirical method for improving transformer reliability.
icml-2026-how-out-of-distribution-detect.tldr: A conditional learning theory for transformer outlier detection motivates training with outlier penalties and soft synthetic outliers.

paragraphs: Reducing numerical precision can make large vision-language models cheaper to run, but it can also damage accuracy. ImpQuant addresses the fact that multimodal inputs contain unevenly distributed information. Errors affecting tokens that matter directly to a decision can be more consequential than errors elsewhere, so calibration should account for their importance.

The method reweights the calibration loss differently for text and images. It uses aggregated attention to assess textual tokens and contextual redundancy to assess visual tokens. It also incorporates activation quantization that accounts for outliers. These components tailor post-training quantization to multimodal information rather than treating the entire input sequence as homogeneous.

Across multiple vision-language backbones and multimodal benchmarks, ImpQuant improves accuracy at low bitwidth compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization baselines. It also reduces object hallucinations induced by quantization in those evaluations. The findings connect numerical compression to the preservation of decision-critical information, showing why attention to token importance can matter for both task accuracy and the fidelity of generated descriptions.
icml-2026-impquant-fine-grained-importan.tldr: ImpQuant prioritizes decision-critical text and image tokens during quantization, improving low-bit accuracy and reducing quantization-induced object hallucinations.

paragraphs: Hyper-Connections introduce challenges in training stability and scalability. Manifold-constrained variants address them by restricting residual connection matrices, but their implementations have costs. An iterative projection may fail to produce exactly doubly stochastic matrices, while an alternative exact parameterization has factorial parameter growth. KromHC seeks both an exact constraint and a more manageable parameter count.

Its central construction combines smaller doubly stochastic matrices through Kronecker products. Constraints are enforced on the factors along the modes of a tensorized residual stream, guaranteeing that the resulting residual matrices remain exactly doubly stochastic. This replaces the expensive full parameterization with a structured composition of smaller constrained components.

The resulting parameter complexity is O(n²C), compared with O(n³C) for mHC and O(nC·n!) for mHC-lite, where n is residual-stream width and C is feature dimension. Experiments show performance matching or exceeding other state-of-the-art mHC variants with substantially fewer trainable parameters. The contribution is an exact structural guarantee paired with improved scaling and competitive empirical performance.
icml-2026-kromhc-manifold-constrained-hy.tldr: KromHC uses Kronecker products to guarantee doubly stochastic residual matrices with lower parameter complexity.

paragraphs: Embodied agents working with partial information can act in ways that conflict with their partners or the environment. LLawCo addresses this coordination problem by learning high-level behavioral rules from previous failures. The aim is to make agents' reasoning better reflect both shared task goals and what other agents are doing.

The framework first identifies patterns of misaligned behavior through reflection on failed attempts. It converts those patterns into cooperation laws, such as communicating when needed or waiting for a partner. Supervised fine-tuning then explicitly incorporates the laws into agents' reasoning chains. This connects lessons from failures to the reasoning used during subsequent cooperative tasks.

The paper also introduces PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale benchmark for communicative, cooperative planning built on PARTNR. Across four language-model backbones, LLawCo reports average success-rate improvements of 4.5% on PARTNR-Dialog and 6.8% on TDW-MAT over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks. The experiments also show improved cooperation efficiency, supporting learned behavioral rules as a useful training signal for the evaluated multi-agent settings.
icml-2026-llawco-learning-laws-of-cooper.tldr: LLawCo turns past coordination failures into behavioral rules and trains embodied agents to apply them during cooperative reasoning.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different views of data to form useful groups. Missing views remove information, while misalignment makes it unclear which samples correspond across views. OPTION addresses these obstacles through learned recovery of missing information and structural alignment of representations, allowing cross-view information to support clustering.

For missing-view recovery, conditional flow matching learns deterministic transport paths intended to preserve the data manifold and produce discriminative representations. For fusion without known sample alignment, a Gromov-Wasserstein-inspired regularizer aligns the internal geometric structures of views in latent space. This avoids requiring hard cross-view correspondences. When samples are aligned, an optional contrastive regularizer can further encourage consistency.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods in ideal, incomplete, and unaligned scenarios, which are evaluated separately. That distinction matters when interpreting the results: the abstract reports evidence across those individual settings rather than a joint evaluation of every difficulty at once. The overall contribution combines missing-view imputation and structural consistency within one clustering method, with an additional mechanism tailored specifically to aligned data.
icml-2026-option-optimal-transportguided.tldr: OPTION combines flow-based missing-view recovery with geometric alignment to improve clustering across separately evaluated incomplete and unaligned settings.

paragraphs: Detecting generated images becomes harder when the relevant clues are subtle and the dominant image content looks convincing. This paper argues that global image representations can overshadow small discriminative signals. Peak-Guided Calibration addresses that problem by giving particularly informative local features a stronger role in the final decision.

PGC uses peak-sensitive aggregation to emphasize local clues that best distinguish generated images. Those aggregated signals then calibrate the detector's global decision. The method therefore connects local evidence with image-level judgment, aiming to recover patterns that would otherwise be submerged by the main subject or other high-fidelity content.

The researchers also introduce CommGen15, containing samples from 15 commercial generative models, to provide a challenging evaluation setting. They report a 12.3% improvement in mean accuracy on this dataset and gains of 2.1% on GenImage, 3.5% on AIGI, and 1.7% on UniversalFakeDetect. These state-of-the-art reported results support the usefulness of emphasizing subtle local signals across the evaluated benchmarks, alongside the contribution of a new commercial-model benchmark.
icml-2026-pgc-peak-guided-calibration-fo.tldr: PGC strengthens generated-image detection by using discriminative local feature peaks to calibrate global decisions.

paragraphs: Point clouds are sparse, lack a regular structure, and can change substantially in representation when rotated. Learning robust features from them can therefore require considerable computation and many parameters. QPoint uses quaternion-based feature learning to address these difficulties in a lightweight framework for point-cloud processing.

The framework combines local and global mechanisms. Its local perception module uses learnable rotations to stabilize features against geometric transformations. Its global attention mechanism uses quaternion similarity to capture broader geometric context with inherent rotation invariance. Together, these components address both the stability of nearby geometric features and the relationships needed to understand the overall shape.

Reported results include 95.0%, 93.9%, and 92.1% on three ScanObjectNN variants, 94.7% overall accuracy on ModelNet40, and 87.0% instance mIoU on ShapeNetParts. The paper also reports stronger generalization in few-shot learning settings. These results are achieved with very small parameter and computational requirements, supporting quaternion-based representations as an efficient foundation for the classification and segmentation evaluations described.
icml-2026-qpoint-end-to-end-lightweight-.tldr: QPoint combines quaternion-based local features and global attention for efficient, rotation-robust point-cloud processing.

paragraphs: Reparameterization policy gradients learn actions by propagating gradients through differentiable system dynamics. Previous approaches have largely used Gaussian policies, limiting their use of newer generative models. This paper connects the approach to flow policies, which produce actions through differentiable ordinary differential equation integration, but finds that a naive combination can be unstable and explore poorly.

Reparameterization Flow Policy Optimization backpropagates through both action generation and system dynamics. This lets it train flow policies without requiring intractable action log-likelihood calculations. Two specialized regularization terms address training stability and exploration, and an additional variant uses action chunking. The method thus develops the optimization machinery needed to make the connection practically useful.

Experiments cover locomotion and manipulation with rigid and soft bodies, using either state information or visual inputs. The reported results demonstrate effectiveness across these settings. On a challenging soft-body quadruped locomotion task, RFO achieves almost twice the reward of the state-of-the-art baseline. That standout comparison is task-specific, while the broader experiments support the approach across the evaluated control problems.
icml-2026-reparameterization-flow-policy.tldr: RFO trains flow-based action policies through differentiable dynamics, using targeted regularization to improve stability and exploration.

paragraphs: Reparameterization policy gradients can learn efficiently from samples by using differentiable dynamics. However, they can underuse expensive dynamics Jacobians and suffer from unstable training. Reusing samples could extract more value from those calculations, but doing so without a principled update rule can make instability worse.

This paper develops Reparameterization Proximal Policy Optimization around a theoretical connection: with sample reuse, reparameterization policy gradients naturally optimize a PPO-style surrogate objective through backpropagation through time. The connection provides a common framework for on-policy and off-policy updates. It supplies a principled basis for reuse rather than treating previously collected samples as interchangeable with fresh ones.

RPO adds a clipped policy-gradient mechanism designed for reparameterization gradients and explicit Kullback-Leibler divergence regularization to improve stability. Experiments across diverse tasks report strong sample efficiency and performance that exceeds or matches the state of the art. The contribution brings together sample reuse and update control, addressing the two problems that motivated the method within one optimization framework.
icml-2026-reparameterization-proximal-po.tldr: RPO provides a principled sample-reuse framework for reparameterization policy gradients and stabilizes updates with clipping and divergence regularization.

paragraphs: Flow matching can train generative models on curved spaces without simulating trajectories during training, yet generating samples typically still requires numerical integration. Riemannian MeanFlow targets one-step generation on these spaces. The geometric challenge is that velocity vectors belong to tangent spaces that depend on location, complicating the definition of an average velocity.

RMF uses parallel transport to define an average-velocity field and derives an identity relating average and instantaneous velocities. A log-map tangent representation makes that identity practical for supervision while avoiding trajectory simulation and heavy geometric calculations. This supplies the geometric machinery needed to extend MeanFlow beyond ordinary flat-space generation.

For more stable optimization, the method divides its objective into two terms and applies conflict-aware multi-task learning to reduce interference between their gradients. It also supports conditional generation through classifier-free guidance. Experiments on spheres, tori, SO(3), and SE(3) demonstrate competitive one-step sampling, improved quality–efficiency trade-offs, and substantially lower sampling cost, supporting the approach across the evaluated manifold geometries.
icml-2026-riemannian-meanflow-for-one-st.tldr: Riemannian MeanFlow adapts average-velocity learning to curved spaces for competitive one-step generation with reduced sampling cost.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer energy-saving computation on neuromorphic hardware, but their non-differentiable spikes complicate self-supervised training. SpikeCLR introduces a fully self-supervised framework for large-scale visual learning without requiring labeled fine-tuning. It uses the timing of spikes as part of the learning signal, aligning representations across both time steps and augmented views.

Its MixedLIF neuron combines a spiking path with an antiderivative-based surrogate path during training to address gradient mismatch and stabilize optimization. At inference, the architecture remains fully spiking. Two additional objectives, Cross Temporal Loss and Boundary Temporal Loss, align outputs across multiple time steps to improve learning efficiency.

Experiments cover ResNet-based and Vision Transformer-based spiking networks on static and neuromorphic datasets. The framework achieves competitive performance and transfers representations learned on ImageNet-1K to downstream tasks. Some resulting self-supervised spiking models match or exceed some non-spiking self-supervised models. These findings support the representational potential of spike-based learning while retaining the inference architecture associated with its energy advantages.
icml-2026-spikeclr-self-supervised-contr.tldr: SpikeCLR uses temporal alignment and a training-time surrogate neuron path to learn strong visual representations while retaining fully spiking inference.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can become severely unstable when trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. This paper traces the problem to importance ratios computed from finite-sample likelihood estimates. Their noise can trigger large gradient spikes and policy drift, which then increase the variance of later ratio estimates, creating a self-reinforcing instability loop.

StableDRL addresses that loop through two mechanisms. Unconditional clipping suppresses spikes caused by outliers, while self-normalization constrains the combined gradient to the convex hull of individual sample updates. Together, these changes control how noisy estimates influence training. A staircase attention mechanism extends the framework to models that generate through block-wise diffusion.

The paper supports its diagnosis with theory and empirical evidence and reports stable full-parameter reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. It reports improvements over the previous best full-attention baselines of 6% on MATH500 and over block-diffusion baselines of 25.6% on AIME. These comparisons connect the stability intervention to stronger reasoning performance in the evaluated settings, rather than treating stable optimization as an isolated outcome.
icml-2026-stabilizing-reinforcement-lear.tldr: StableDRL controls noisy importance-ratio updates to stabilize reinforcement learning and improve evaluated diffusion-language-model reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Code can pass functional tests while failing to satisfy what a user requested about how the solution should be written. This paper hypothesizes that instruction following helps explain human preferences beyond correctness alone. It investigates that idea by making non-functional code instructions measurable rather than relying only on whether generated programs work.

The researchers introduce VeriCode, a taxonomy of 30 verifiable code instructions paired with deterministic checkers. They use it to augment established evaluation suites, creating SWE-IF. The resulting testbed assesses functional correctness and instruction compliance together, making it possible to examine whether satisfying additional requests comes at the expense of working code.

Evaluation of 31 language models shows that even the strongest struggle with multiple instructions and exhibit functional regression. A composite score combining correctness and instruction following correlates best with human preference, with instruction following providing the main distinction among models. The findings support broader code evaluation that measures both what the program does and how faithfully it follows the user's requirements.
icml-2026-swe-if-aligning-code-evaluatio.tldr: SWE-IF evaluates code instruction following alongside correctness, producing a combined measure that better correlates with human preference.

paragraphs: Large 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions require storing attributes for enormous numbers of Gaussian primitives, quickly exceeding GPU memory. TideGS exploits the observation that each training iteration uses only primitives visible from its current camera batch. GPU memory can therefore hold the active working set while the larger parameter collection resides elsewhere.

The framework manages parameters across SSD storage, CPU memory, and GPU memory. It groups geometry into blocks suited to SSD access, overlaps data movement with computation through an asynchronous hierarchy, and adapts streaming to the camera trajectory. By transferring only changes in the working set between iterations, it avoids repeatedly moving all active parameters.

Experiments demonstrate training with more than one billion Gaussians on a single 24-GB GPU. TideGS also achieves the best reconstruction quality among the evaluated single-GPU baselines on large scenes, scaling beyond the cited out-of-core and in-memory comparisons. The results show how exploiting visibility and camera-dependent reuse can make storage capacity outside the GPU useful for substantially larger training problems.
icml-2026-tidegs-scalable-training-of-ov.tldr: TideGS streams active Gaussian parameters across SSD, CPU, and GPU memory to train billion-primitive scenes on one 24-GB GPU.

paragraphs: Coding agents can edit and test complex software yet still misunderstand what a user wants when instructions depend on context or omit details. ToM-SWE addresses this by pairing a software-engineering agent with a lightweight partner dedicated to modeling the user's goals, constraints, and preferences.

The partner draws on instructions and interaction history, maintains persistent user memory, and supplies relevant suggestions to the coding agent. The architecture is designed to preserve privacy and reduce context-window load while keeping user-related information available across interactions. This makes ongoing user understanding a distinct responsibility within the agent system.

The paper reports improved task success and user satisfaction on ambiguous and stateful software-engineering benchmarks. On the new stateful benchmark, which includes a user simulator and previous interaction histories, ToM-SWE reaches 59.7% success compared with 18.1% for OpenHands. In a three-week study with professional developers, participants found it better aligned with their intent and useful 86% of the time. Together, these evaluations support persistent user modeling as a practical addition to coding capability.
icml-2026-tom-swe-user-mental-modeling-f.tldr: ToM-SWE adds a persistent user-modeling partner to a coding agent, improving reported task success and alignment with developer intent.
